cues.text: A Faith Korea Discovered for Itself
Christianity reached Korea by a path almost unique in the whole history of Catholic missions, not through foreign missionaries first arriving on Korean soil.
Instead, Korean scholars traveled to China, encountered Catholic texts translated into Chinese, and carried the faith home themselves, establishing a genuine Christian community.
It grew for years under entirely lay leadership before a single ordained priest ever entered the country.

Those first Korean Christians baptized one another using whatever knowledge of the sacraments their smuggled texts could provide, developing a genuinely indigenous Church years before Rome itself had any formal awareness that Korean converts existed at all.
A Confucian Court's Suspicion
Korea's ruling Confucian establishment viewed this new faith's rejection of traditional ancestor veneration rites as a direct and dangerous challenge to the social order itself.
Repeated waves of persecution followed across the early nineteenth century as the government sought to suppress a religion it regarded as fundamentally incompatible with Korean tradition.
The Gihae Persecution of 1839
The first major wave to claim significant numbers of both foreign and native believers broke out in 1839.

The French bishop Laurent Imbert and two fellow missionary priests, learning that their own capture might spare the wider community further violence, voluntarily surrendered themselves to authorities.
They were beheaded alongside numerous Korean Catholics, including the lay leader Paul Chong Hasang.
The three martyred missionaries chose surrender deliberately, reasoning that the persecution's fury might exhaust itself on their own capture.
They hoped this would prevent its spread among the Korean laity who had sheltered them—a hope only partly realized, since hundreds of ordinary believers were executed in the same wave regardless.
The First Native Priest, Martyred
Korea's very first ordained native priest, Andrew Kim Taegon , trained abroad, in the complete absence of any seminary within his own closed homeland.

He returned in 1845, only to be arrested and beheaded the following year at just twenty-five, having completed barely a year of active ministry among the very people he had crossed a continent to serve.

Kim's own final letter to his scattered flock, urging perseverance regardless of what befell him personally, was copied and passed hand to hand among Korean Catholics for years afterward as a treasured source of courage.
The Great Persecution of 1866
The bloodiest of all the waves came in 1866, under the regency of the Heungseon Daewongun.
Rising fears of Western intrusion following armed incidents along the Korean coast hardened into a sustained campaign.

It claimed two bishops, numerous French missionaries, and an estimated eight to ten thousand Korean Catholic laypeople over the following six years, before persecution gradually subsided toward the end of the century.

Catholics who survived the worst of this final wave fled into remote mountain villages, continuing to practice their faith in secret hamlets that would not see an openly functioning parish church again for over a decade.
Legacy
Altogether more than ten thousand Korean Catholics are believed to have died across nearly a century of intermittent persecution, stretching from 1791 to the 1870s.
The overwhelming majority were ordinary laypeople rather than clergy — men and women, married and unmarried, old and young.
They belonged to a Church whose founding and endurance owed more to lay faith than to any missionary institution.

In 1984, Pope John Paul II canonized 103 of these martyrs together in Seoul, the first canonization ceremony ever held outside Rome, honoring a Church that had, from its very beginning, belonged first and always to its own ordinary believers.

Korea today counts among the countries with the largest number of canonized saints in the entire Catholic world, a legacy this same persecuted, largely leaderless community first built almost entirely on its own.
